topic: Day 1 · Intrinsic Renal AKI — AIN, Glomerular & Vascular
speakerBio: Nephrologist and glomerulonephritis lead who runs the hospital's urine microscopy teaching clinic and insists every trainee spins their own patient's sample before phoning the on-call renal registrar.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 58-year-old man is admitted with a week of malaise, a faint rash over his trunk, and a creatinine that has climbed from a baseline of 80 to 340 µmol/L. He is not hypotensive, not obstructed, and euvolaemic — so the two easy answers (pre-renal and post-renal) are already off the table. His urine dipstick shows blood ++ and protein +, and under the microscope the lab reports red cell casts. Someone on the round mutters "acute tubular necrosis." Stop. ATN does not make red cell casts. This patient has an intrinsic renal parenchymal disease, and the exact compartment it lives in — tubulointerstitium, glomerulus, or microvasculature — is written in his urine sediment. This is the session where the urine becomes a biopsy you can read in ninety seconds.

1 · 🧭 Framing intrinsic AKI — which compartment is on fire?

Once you have excluded a pre-renal (perfusion) and a post-renal (obstruction) cause, "intrinsic AKI" is not a diagnosis — it is four anatomically distinct diseases that happen to share a rising creatinine. The kidney has four compartments and each fails in its own way:

CompartmentDisease bucketSediment signatureSpeed
TubulesAcute tubular necrosis (ischaemic/toxic)Muddy-brown granular casts, renal tubular epithelial cellsDays
InterstitiumAcute interstitial nephritis (AIN)Sterile pyuria, WBC casts, eosinophiluriaDays–weeks
GlomerulusRapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN)Dysmorphic RBCs, red cell casts, proteinuriaDays–weeks (emergency)
MicrovasculatureThrombotic microangiopathy, atheroemboli, vasculitisSchistocytes on film; bland or active sedimentHours–days
ATN gives muddy-brown granular casts. Red cell casts mean glomerulonephritis. White cell casts mean interstitial nephritis. The sediment names the compartment.
💡 The liquid biopsy

A properly spun, freshly examined urine sediment is the cheapest, fastest renal biopsy you will ever order — and it is available at 3 a.m. when the histopathologist is not. Look yourself: a fresh, warm, unspun-then-spun sample examined within the hour, before casts dissolve. The nephrologist you phone will ask "what did the sediment show?" before anything else.

2 · 🔬 The urine sediment — reading the liquid biopsy

Spin 10 mL of fresh urine at low speed, decant, resuspend the pellet, and look under low and high power. What you find sorts the differential faster than any blood test:

Sediment findingPoints toMechanism
Muddy-brown granular castsAcute tubular necrosisSloughed, degenerating tubular epithelial cells packed into a Tamm–Horsfall matrix
Red cell casts + dysmorphic RBCsGlomerulonephritis / RPGNRBCs squeezed through a damaged glomerular basement membrane, moulded in the tubule
White cell casts + sterile pyuriaAcute interstitial nephritis (also pyelonephritis)Inflammatory cells trafficking through an inflamed interstitium
EosinophiluriaAIN (weak), also atheroemboliHansel/Wright stain — poor sensitivity and specificity
Free tubular epithelial cells / RTE castsATNDirect tubular injury
"Bland" sediment (nothing)Pre-renal, obstruction, vascular, myelomaNo parenchymal inflammation
Dysmorphic RBCs (acanthocytes)Glomerular bleedingMembrane damage crossing the GBM — the "Mickey Mouse" G1 cell
🎯 Dysmorphic vs isomorphic haematuria

Where is the blood coming from? Dysmorphic RBCs (irregular, budding acanthocytes) and red cell casts mean the blood crossed the glomerulus — a medical, nephritic problem. Isomorphic (uniform, normal-shaped) RBCs mean the blood entered downstream — stones, tumour, infection — a urological problem that gets a cystoscopy and a CT urogram, not immunosuppression. One microscope slide decides which specialty owns the patient.

3 · 💊 Acute interstitial nephritis — the great drug mimic

AIN is a hypersensitivity reaction in the tubulointerstitium: a T-cell–mediated response, usually to a drug, that floods the interstitium with lymphocytes, eosinophils and oedema and squeezes tubular function. It is one of the most reversible intrinsic AKIs — if you stop the culprit early — and one of the most missed, because its classic textbook signs are usually absent.

The offenders — drugs cause ~70–90%

ClassExamplesNote
Proton pump inhibitorsOmeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazoleNow among the commonest causes; onset often weeks–months, insidious
NSAIDsIbuprofen, diclofenac, naproxenCan cause AIN + minimal-change nephrotic syndrome together; little rash/eosinophilia
AntibioticsPenicillins, cephalosporins, rifampicin, ciprofloxacin, sulphonamidesThe classic "allergic" AIN with rash/fever/eosinophilia
OthersAllopurinol, 5-ASA/mesalazine, diuretics, checkpoint inhibitorsImmune checkpoint inhibitor AIN is a fast-rising ICU/oncology cause

The classic triad is a trap

Textbooks teach the triad of fever + rash + eosinophilia. In reality the complete triad is present in fewer than 10% of biopsy-proven cases. Waiting for it is how AIN gets missed for weeks while the culprit drug keeps being administered. Instead, suspect AIN in any unexplained AKI with a compatible drug exposure, especially with:

  • Sterile pyuria — white cells in the urine with a negative culture.
  • White cell casts — the specific interstitial signature.
  • Eosinophiluria — historically emphasised, but poor sensitivity and specificity (also seen in atheroemboli, pyelonephritis, GN); a positive test nudges you, a negative one excludes nothing.
  • Modest sub-nephrotic proteinuria (NSAID-AIN can be nephrotic).
  • Peripheral eosinophilia and a raised CRP.
The classic AIN triad is present in under 10% of cases — so if you wait for the rash, you will miss it. Think AIN in any drug-associated AKI with sterile pyuria or white cell casts.
💡 Gallium and biopsy

The definitive diagnosis is a renal biopsy (interstitial infiltrate + tubulitis, oedema, eosinophils). A Ga-67 scan can light up the inflamed interstitium but is neither sensitive nor specific. In practice: strong suspicion + clear temporal drug link → stop the drug and treat; equivocal or steroid-dependent case → biopsy to confirm before committing to immunosuppression.

Treatment — stop the drug, then steroids

  • Withdraw the culprit immediately — this alone reverses many cases. Recovery begins in days to a couple of weeks.
  • Corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone ~1 mg/kg/day, or IV methylprednisolone pulses in severe disease) if creatinine does not improve after stopping the drug, or if biopsy shows florid inflammation. Earlier steroids (within ~7–14 days) are associated with better renal recovery — delay allows interstitial fibrosis to set, and fibrosis does not come back.
  • Check for chronic interstitial fibrosis on biopsy — heavy fibrosis predicts non-recovery and argues against steroids.
⚠️ The PPI that was "harmless"

A 71-year-old woman had lansoprazole started three months earlier for reflux. Her creatinine drifted from 70 to 190 over eight weeks and was repeatedly attributed to "her age" and "a bit of dehydration." No one examined the urine. By the time a nephrologist saw sterile pyuria and white cell casts and stopped the PPI, the biopsy showed established interstitial fibrosis and she never recovered below a creatinine of 150. PPI-AIN is insidious and painless — there is no rash to warn you. Review the drug chart in every unexplained subacute AKI.

4 · 🔥 Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis — a nephrological emergency

RPGN is the clinical syndrome of a nephritic presentation — haematuria with dysmorphic RBCs and red cell casts, hypertension, oedema, sub-nephrotic-to-nephrotic proteinuria — with a creatinine that doubles over days to a few weeks. The histological correlate is crescents: proliferating epithelial cells and macrophages filling Bowman's space, strangling the glomerulus. Untreated, crescents organise into scar within weeks and the nephron is lost forever. This is the one intrinsic AKI where a delay of days changes the outcome from dialysis-free to dialysis-dependent.

The three immunological patterns (by immunofluorescence)

PatternImmunofluorescenceDiseasesKey serology
Type I — anti-GBMLinear IgG along the GBMGoodpasture (kidney + lung)Anti-GBM antibody positive
Type II — immune complexGranular ("lumpy-bumpy")Lupus nephritis, IgA/HSP, post-infectious, cryoglobulinaemicANA/dsDNA, low complement, ASOT, IgA
Type III — pauci-immuneScanty/no depositsANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA, MPA, EGPA)c-ANCA/PR3, p-ANCA/MPO

The pulmonary–renal syndromes — kidney and lung together

When haemoptysis or alveolar haemorrhage accompanies a nephritic AKI, three diagnoses dominate and all are treatable emergencies:

  • Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture) — antibodies to the α3 chain of type IV collagen, shared by glomerular and alveolar basement membrane. Bimodal (young men with lung haemorrhage; older adults with isolated GN). Treat with plasma exchange (to remove antibody) plus steroids and cyclophosphamide. Speed is everything — patients presenting oligo-anuric or dialysis-dependent rarely recover renal function, so this is a same-day diagnosis.
  • ANCA-associated vasculitis — granulomatosis with polyangiitis (PR3/c-ANCA, ENT + lung + kidney), microscopic polyangiitis (MPO/p-ANCA), eosinophilic GPA. The commonest cause of pauci-immune RPGN. Treat with high-dose steroids + rituximab or cyclophosphamide; plasma exchange reserved (per PEXIVAS) for severe pulmonary haemorrhage or very severe renal disease.
  • Lupus nephritis — immune-complex GN; class III/IV proliferative disease presents with an active nephritic sediment. Treat with steroids plus mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide (± belimumab/voclosporin).
Nephritic sediment + haemoptysis = a pulmonary–renal syndrome until proven otherwise: send anti-GBM, ANCA, ANA/dsDNA and complement today, and phone nephrology before the bloods are back.
🎯 The "renal emergency screen"

Any AKI with an active urinary sediment gets an immediate immunology panel: ANCA (PR3/MPO), anti-GBM, ANA and anti-dsDNA, complement C3/C4, cryoglobulins, ASOT/anti-DNase, immunoglobulins and serum free light chains, hepatitis B/C serology, and blood film. Combined with the sediment, this panel plus an urgent biopsy directs immunosuppression. Do not wait for the biopsy to send the serology — the assays take days.

Treatment principle — do not wait

Crescentic GN is treated with urgent immunosuppression: pulsed IV methylprednisolone, then cyclophosphamide or rituximab, with plasma exchange for anti-GBM and selected severe vasculitis/pulmonary haemorrhage. Empirical high-dose steroids are often started the moment the picture is convincing, before the biopsy, because a week of delay is the difference between recovered nephrons and fibrous scars.

5 · 🩸 Thrombotic microangiopathy — the microvascular AKI

TMA is endothelial injury driving platelet-fibrin thrombi in the microvasculature. The clinical signature is a mechanical (microangiopathic) haemolytic anaemia: schistocytes on the blood film, a high LDH, low haptoglobin, thrombocytopenia, and organ injury — prominently the kidney. Coombs test is negative (this is mechanical, not immune, haemolysis).

SyndromeMechanismClueTreatment
Typical HUSShiga-toxin (E. coli O157) → endothelial injuryBloody diarrhoea, children; renal-dominantSupportive; usually self-limiting
Atypical HUSComplement dysregulationNo diarrhoea, relapsing, family historyEculizumab (anti-C5)
TTPADAMTS13 deficiency → large vWF multimersNeuro signs, fever, more CNS than renalPlasma exchange — emergency; ± caplacizumab, rituximab
Secondary TMADrugs (calcineurin inhibitors, gemcitabine, quinine), pregnancy (HELLP), malignant hypertension, scleroderma renal crisisContext-dependentTreat the trigger (e.g. ACE-i in scleroderma crisis)
⚠️ Never transfuse platelets into TTP for the low count alone

The thrombocytopenia in TTP is consumptive from microvascular thrombosis, not a bleeding problem. Pouring in platelets "to correct the number" can fuel further thrombosis and precipitate stroke or death. TTP with a pentad or even a dyad (MAHA + thrombocytopenia with no other cause) is a plasma-exchange emergency — start PLEX the same day and send an ADAMTS13 level, do not wait for it to come back. The pentad (MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neuro signs, fever, renal failure) is present in full in a minority — treat on the dyad.

💡 One film changes everything

Any AKI with a falling platelet count deserves a blood film that day. Schistocytes + thrombocytopenia = TMA, and TMA reframes the whole admission: it is no longer "ATN, wait and see" but a haematological emergency needing plasma exchange (TTP), eculizumab (aHUS) or urgent trigger control.

6 · 🟡 Atheroembolic (cholesterol crystal) disease — the great mimic

Cholesterol crystals shower from an ulcerated aortic plaque into small arteries, days to weeks after an arterial insult — angiography/PCI, vascular surgery, or anticoagulation/thrombolysis. The result is a subacute, stuttering AKI that classically declines in steps over weeks, not the abrupt injury of contrast nephropathy.

  • Peripheral stigmata: livedo reticularis, blue toes with intact pulses, retinal Hollenhorst plaques, digital gangrene, abdominal pain.
  • Labs: transient eosinophilia and eosinophiluria, low complement, raised inflammatory markers — a great mimic of vasculitis (but ANCA/anti-GBM negative).
  • Timing distinguishes it from contrast-induced AKI: contrast nephropathy peaks at 3–5 days and recovers; atheroemboli begin 1–4 weeks after the procedure and often do not recover.
Blue toes with palpable pulses + a rising creatinine weeks after an angiogram = cholesterol emboli, not contrast nephropathy.

Treatment is supportive: statins, risk-factor control, avoid further arterial instrumentation and (where possible) further anticoagulation. There is no specific therapy; prognosis is guarded. Skin or renal biopsy shows the pathognomonic biconvex cholesterol clefts.

7 · 🧮 The master table — sediment to diagnosis

This is the single grid to memorise. Match the sediment column to the compartment and you have your differential before the biopsy:

Sediment / clueCompartmentLeading diagnosisNext test / action
Muddy-brown granular casts, RTE cellsTubuleAcute tubular necrosisSupportive; look for ischaemic/toxic trigger
WBC casts, sterile pyuria, eosinophiluriaInterstitiumAcute interstitial nephritisStop culprit drug; consider steroids/biopsy
Red cell casts, dysmorphic RBCs, proteinuriaGlomerulusRPGN / glomerulonephritisRenal emergency screen + urgent biopsy + immunosuppression
Nephritic sediment + haemoptysisGlomerulus + lungAnti-GBM / ANCA / lupusAnti-GBM, ANCA, ANA/dsDNA, complement TODAY; PLEX for anti-GBM
Schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, high LDHMicrovasculatureTMA (HUS/TTP)Blood film, ADAMTS13, LDH/haptoglobin; PLEX for TTP
Blue toes, livedo, eosinophilia, weeks post-angiogramMicrovasculatureCholesterol emboliSupportive; statin; avoid further instrumentation
Bland sediment + high creatinine + bone pain/anaemiaTubule (cast nephropathy)MyelomaSerum free light chains, SPEP/urine electrophoresis
🎯 Don't forget myeloma cast nephropathy

An older patient with an unexplained AKI, a bland sediment, anaemia, hypercalcaemia and bone pain — think multiple myeloma. Free light chains obstruct and injure tubules ("cast nephropathy"), and the standard urine dipstick misses light chains (it detects albumin, not Bence-Jones protein). Send serum free light chains and protein electrophoresis. It is the intrinsic AKI hiding behind a normal-looking urine.

8 · 🧑‍⚕️ Back to our patient

The 58-year-old man with red cell casts, dysmorphic haematuria and a doubling creatinine had a nephritic sediment — glomerular disease. The renal emergency screen returned a positive MPO/p-ANCA with normal complement and negative anti-GBM. An urgent biopsy showed a pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis — ANCA-associated (microscopic polyangiitis). He was started on pulsed methylprednisolone and rituximab within 48 hours of the sediment result and recovered to a creatinine of 130 — dialysis-free. Had the round's initial call of "ATN, wait and see" stood, the crescents would have scarred and he would have needed lifelong dialysis. The urine told the truth before the biopsy did.

9 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Intrinsic AKI is four diseases, not one — tubule, interstitium, glomerulus, microvasculature — and the urine sediment tells you which.
  2. Cast rules: muddy-brown granular = ATN; white cell casts = AIN; red cell casts + dysmorphic RBCs = glomerulonephritis.
  3. AIN is a drug diagnosis (PPIs, NSAIDs, antibiotics), the classic triad is present in <10%, and the treatment is stop the drug early ± steroids — before fibrosis sets.
  4. RPGN is an emergency: nephritic sediment + doubling creatinine = crescents. Send ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA/dsDNA and complement the same day and start immunosuppression early.
  5. Nephritic sediment + haemoptysis = a pulmonary–renal syndrome — anti-GBM (plasma exchange), ANCA vasculitis, or lupus.
  6. Schistocytes + thrombocytopenia = TMA; TTP is a same-day plasma-exchange emergency and you never transfuse platelets for the count alone.
  7. Blue toes with pulses weeks after an angiogram = cholesterol emboli, not contrast nephropathy — timing separates them.
  8. A bland sediment with an unexplained AKI in an older patient → send free light chains; myeloma hides behind normal urine.

moderatorQs.q: A patient on omeprazole has an unexplained AKI but no fever, rash or eosinophilia. Can you exclude acute interstitial nephritis?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: No — absolutely not. The classic triad of fever, rash and eosinophilia is present in fewer than 10% of biopsy-proven AIN, and PPI-induced AIN in particular is characteristically insidious and painless with none of those features. The findings that should actually raise suspicion are sterile pyuria, white cell casts and modest proteinuria in the context of a compatible drug. The correct move is to examine the urine sediment, stop the likely culprit, and — if the creatinine does not improve or the picture is florid — consider a renal biopsy and early corticosteroids. Waiting for the textbook triad is precisely how AIN is missed until irreversible interstitial fibrosis has developed.

moderatorQs.q: You find red cell casts and a creatinine that has doubled in a week. Why is this a medical emergency and what happens if you wait for the biopsy?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Red cell casts with a rapidly rising creatinine define rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, whose histological substrate is crescents — proliferating cells filling Bowman's space. Crescents organise into irreversible fibrous scar within a few weeks, so every day of delay converts recoverable nephrons into permanent loss and can be the difference between dialysis-free survival and lifelong dialysis. Because the immunology assays (ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA/dsDNA, complement) take days to return and the biopsy adds further delay, the correct approach is to send the full renal emergency screen the same day, arrange an urgent biopsy, and frequently start empirical high-dose pulsed methylprednisolone before the biopsy result when the clinical picture is convincing.

moderatorQs.q: A patient develops AKI, thrombocytopenia and schistocytes on the film. Walk me through how you distinguish and manage the thrombotic microangiopathies.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Schistocytes plus thrombocytopenia with a high LDH, low haptoglobin and negative Coombs establishes a microangiopathic (mechanical) haemolytic anaemia — a TMA. The subtypes: TTP (ADAMTS13 deficiency, more neurological than renal) is a same-day plasma-exchange emergency — start PLEX and send an ADAMTS13 level, do not wait for it. Typical HUS follows Shiga-toxin diarrhoea in children and is largely supportive. Atypical HUS (complement dysregulation) is treated with eculizumab. Secondary TMA from drugs (calcineurin inhibitors, gemcitabine, quinine), malignant hypertension, HELLP or scleroderma renal crisis is managed by treating the trigger. Critically, you never transfuse platelets into TTP for the low count alone — it fuels further thrombosis.

audienceQs.q: How do I tell whether haematuria is a kidney problem or a bladder/urology problem at the bedside?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Look at the red cells under the microscope and look for casts. Dysmorphic red cells (irregular, budding acanthocytes — the 'Mickey Mouse' cells) and red cell casts mean the blood crossed the glomerulus — a medical, nephritic problem that gets an immunology screen and often a biopsy. Isomorphic red cells (uniform, normal-shaped) with no casts, especially with clots or visible frank haematuria, point downstream to stones, tumour or infection — a urological problem needing imaging (CT urogram) and cystoscopy. Proteinuria alongside the blood also argues strongly for a glomerular (nephritic) source. One well-examined sediment usually tells you which specialty owns the patient.

audienceQs.q: Which drugs on a patient's chart should make me think about acute interstitial nephritis?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The big three classes are proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole, lansoprazole — now among the commonest and most insidious causes), NSAIDs (which can also cause a concurrent minimal-change nephrotic picture), and antibiotics — penicillins, cephalosporins, rifampicin, ciprofloxacin and sulphonamides. Also flag allopurinol, mesalazine/5-ASA, diuretics and increasingly immune checkpoint inhibitors. In any unexplained AKI with sterile pyuria I'd review the chart for a temporally-related new drug and recommend stopping the likely culprit, because early withdrawal is what determines whether the kidney recovers before interstitial fibrosis sets in.

audienceQs.q: A patient's creatinine keeps climbing in steps three weeks after a coronary angiogram, with blue toes but good pulses. Isn't this just contrast nephropathy?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The timing and the toes make this cholesterol atheroembolic disease, not contrast-induced AKI. Contrast nephropathy peaks at 3–5 days and typically recovers; atheroemboli begin 1–4 weeks after arterial instrumentation and decline in a stuttering, stepwise fashion. The blue toes with palpable pulses, plus livedo reticularis, transient eosinophilia/eosinophiluria and low complement, are the giveaway (and it mimics vasculitis, so ANCA/anti-GBM will be negative). Management is supportive — statin, tight risk-factor control, and avoiding further arterial instrumentation and, where feasible, further anticoagulation. Skin or renal biopsy shows the pathognomonic cholesterol clefts. The prognosis is unfortunately guarded, so prevention (minimising repeat instrumentation) matters most.
